source: Mansoori and Lackeus (2020) Comparing effectuation to discovery-driven planning, prescriptive entrepreneurship, business planning, lean startup, and design thinking
finding: Discovery-driven planning (McGrath and MacMillan 1995, 2000) rests on one idea: uncertainty falls when assumptions are converted into knowledge, and plans are redirected as understanding emerges. Failures come from reliance on untested assumptions.
numbers: Six guideline areas: frame the idea, benchmark success parameters, specify operational deliverables, document and test assumptions, manage milestones, run lean until key assumptions are tested. Tools: reverse income statement, targeted experiments, assumptions checklist.
limits: A conceptual comparison of six methods, not an empirical test. The authors treat the literature as quasi-data.
agent_relevance: Maps onto S7: the plan becomes a list of assumptions, and each is tested before more resources are spent.

source: Mansoori and Lackeus (2020) Comparing effectuation to discovery-driven planning, prescriptive entrepreneurship, business planning, lean startup, and design thinking
finding: The reverse income statement starts from the required profit and works back to what must be true (volume, price, cost). This turns a forecast into a checklist of assumptions with checkpoints.
numbers: Method has ten steps; the assumptions checklist is revisited at each milestone.
limits: Secondary description. The primary 1995 HBR article was not opened.
agent_relevance: For our agent: start from the target answer and list what must hold, which is the same move as O5 (work backwards) applied to a plan.

source: Mansoori and Lackeus (2020) Comparing effectuation to discovery-driven planning, prescriptive entrepreneurship, business planning, lean startup, and design thinking
finding: Compared with lean startup, discovery-driven planning is built for corporate settings and wider uncertainty; lean startup stresses build-measure-learn loops and cheap tests (A/B, fake door, concierge).
numbers: Table 1 lists targeted experiments, A/B tests and fake-door tests as the shared tactic family.
limits: Comparison is qualitative. The paper notes entrepreneurial methods are criticised for lack of rigor.
agent_relevance: The shared core (hypothesis, cheapest test, decision rule) is what to copy, not the branding.

source: Rita McGrath (2024) Who Learns Fastest, Wins: Lean Startup and Discovery Driven Growth (J. of Management 50(8))
finding: Frames discovery-driven growth and lean startup as learning races: both aim at fast learning and cheap failure. Discovery-driven growth is less prescriptive and tolerates wider uncertainty than lean startup, which targets product-market fit.
numbers: None given on the teaser page.
limits: Only the author's teaser page and a search abstract were read; the full text was not accessible. No outcome numbers seen.
agent_relevance: Rank by learning speed and cost, not by prediction accuracy.

source: Camuffo, Cordova, Gambardella and Spina (2020) A scientific approach to entrepreneurial decision making: evidence from a randomized control trial (Management Science)
finding: RCT of 116 Italian startups, 16 data points over about one year. Both arms got 10 sessions (5 lectures of 3.5 h, 5 one-hour mentoring sessions) on market validation. Treated arm spent 30% of time on a scientific approach: frame the problem, write falsifiable hypotheses, test them with set metrics and thresholds. Control arm got 100% standard validation and used its own intuitions.
numbers: N=116 startups, 21 mentors (each with 3 treated and 3 control), 1,856 panel observations.
limits: Small sample. Italian, mostly ordinary (not deep-tech) businesses. Only 17 firms earned any revenue in the window. Control arm may have been taught less in total.
agent_relevance: Cleanest causal test that teaching hypothesis plus threshold testing changes outcomes at equal training hours.

source: Camuffo, Cordova, Gambardella and Spina (2020) A scientific approach to entrepreneurial decision making: evidence from a randomized control trial (Management Science)
finding: Treated startups pivoted more. Pivot count rose (linear coefficient 0.261, p=0.027; negative binomial 0.803, p<0.001; panel 0.016, p=0.033). Seven treated firms pivoted more than once; one control firm did.
numbers: 41 pivots in total across both arms (as reported). 7 treated firms pivoted 2 to 4 times, 1 control firm pivoted twice.
limits: Pivot was measured by phone interviews and self-report, with a definition of 'major change'.
agent_relevance: A scientific approach should lead to more changes of plan, not fewer. An agent that never revises after a test is not testing.

source: Camuffo, Cordova, Gambardella and Spina (2020) A scientific approach to entrepreneurial decision making: evidence from a randomized control trial (Management Science)
finding: Treated startups earned revenue earlier and more. 17 firms earned positive revenue: 9 treated, 8 control, but 85 of the 107 revenue observations came from treated firms (22 from control).
numbers: 9 versus 8 firms, 85 versus 22 observations with revenue; effect positive in cross-section and panel, robust to winsorising and hyperbolic-sine transform.
limits: Revenue effect rests on 17 firms, so it is fragile. Authors say it comes from firms that found a good idea early.
agent_relevance: Value of testing shows as earlier and larger payoffs for the few that pass, not a broad lift.

source: Camuffo, Cordova, Gambardella and Spina (2020) A scientific approach to entrepreneurial decision making: evidence from a randomized control trial (Management Science)
finding: Treated startups were not less likely to drop out over time. Exit coefficient in the cross-section was 0.035 (p=0.045); survival (Cox) p=0.101 and panel p=0.716 were not significant. The authors read this as 'precision', not just 'learning'.
numbers: Self-rated confidence to abandon a startup (1-7 scale, 81 firms): treated 4.4, control 3.2, p<0.01.
limits: Exit is rare (2.2% of panel observations). Authors say they cannot rule out that learning also plays a part.
agent_relevance: A test should make the agent better at killing bad ideas and keeping good ones, so measure both false positives and false negatives.

source: Camuffo, Cordova, Gambardella and Spina (2020) A scientific approach to entrepreneurial decision making: evidence from a randomized control trial (Management Science)
finding: Formal model: an entrepreneur has a prior on idea value, gets a signal, and chooses develop, pivot or exit by a threshold. A scientific approach reduces false positives (bad ideas pursued) and false negatives (good ideas dropped) by improving the precision of the signal.
numbers: Decision rule: develop if expected value v0 is above threshold v*, else pivot. Scientists have a higher threshold and a more conservative reading of the signal.
limits: Model is a stylised setup. Authors did not test whether treated firms eventually fail faster, because the window was too short.
agent_relevance: Gives a decision-theory frame for S7: a test is worth running if it moves the posterior across the act or not-act threshold.

source: Camuffo, Cordova, Gambardella and Spina (2020) A scientific approach to entrepreneurial decision making: evidence from a randomized control trial (Management Science)
finding: Case: Inkdome (tattoo-artist matching). Control-style interviews ('Would you use it?') give polite yes answers. Treated style set four hypotheses with a rule: reject a hypothesis if fewer than 60% of 50 interviews corroborate. Three of four hypotheses passed and the fourth failed; interviews showed the real problem was judging a tattooist's skill.
numbers: Threshold 60%, sample 50 interviews, 4 hypotheses, 1 failed.
limits: Single illustrative case chosen by the authors.
agent_relevance: Shows the mechanism to copy: pre-set threshold before looking, ask about past behaviour not intent, test the weakest assumption first.
quote: reject a hypothesis if less than 60% of their interviews

source: Camuffo, Gambardella, Messinese, Novelli, Paolucci and Spina (2024) A scientific approach to entrepreneurial decision-making: replication in four RCTs (Strategic Management Journal)
finding: Replication and extension reported in a search summary: 759 firms in four randomized trials. Positive effect on idea termination and a non-linear effect on radical pivots (treated firms ran few or no pivots, or repeated ones).
numbers: 759 firms across four RCTs.
limits: Not opened: the repository page was blocked by bot protection. Figures are from a search summary only.
agent_relevance: If it holds, the original result is not a one-off; the pivot effect is not monotone, so more testing does not always mean more pivoting.

source: Koning, Hasan and Chatterji (2022) Experimentation and startup performance: evidence from A/B testing (NBER w26278; Management Science 68(9))
finding: Observational panel of about 35,000 global startups over 173 weeks, using staggered adoption of A/B testing tools (Optimizely, VWO and others). Few firms adopt: 7.6% at the start, 16.75% at some point.
numbers: Adopters had 280% more page views in a raw comparison; 46% after firm fixed effects; 11.8% after controlling for tech-stack size; 8.5% with firm growth slopes. Authors' headline: about 10% more page views.
limits: Not randomised; adopters are selected. The raw 280% was mostly selection, which shows how easily testing looks better than it is. A search snippet for the published version reports 30% to 100% gains after a year; that figure was not checked.
agent_relevance: Even where testing works, the true effect is far below the naive comparison. Budget for modest gains.

source: Koning, Hasan and Chatterji (2022) Experimentation and startup performance: evidence from A/B testing (NBER w26278; Management Science 68(9))
finding: Event study: no pre-trend before adoption; effects appear about one year later (about 8% page-view growth). A/B testing raised product launches by 9% to 18% and raised both tail outcomes.
numbers: Zero page views +0.7 percentage points; 100,000+ page views +1.4 points; 4,645 adopting firms in the event study; new product launches +0.067.
limits: Page views are a proxy for performance. Digital firms only.
agent_relevance: Cheap tests make more ideas get tried and make failure faster, which fits the idea of testing cheaply and in order of cost.

source: Koning, Hasan and Chatterji (2022) Experimentation and startup performance: evidence from A/B testing (NBER w26278; Management Science 68(9))
finding: Benefits depend on the firm. Younger ventures fail faster; older firms are more likely to scale; firms with experienced managers gain more.
numbers: Effect sizes on some outcomes range from 1.4% to 5.5% (as reported).
limits: Moderator results are observational.
agent_relevance: The same test tool helps unevenly; skill at reading the test matters, not just running it.

source: Wason (1960) On the failure to eliminate hypotheses in a conceptual task, as described in Jhaveri et al. (2026)
finding: Original 2-4-6 task: people are told 2-4-6 fits a hidden rule (any increasing triple) and propose triples to test. Most propose triples that fit their narrow guess (for example +2 steps), get yes, and announce a wrong rule.
numbers: 29 participants: 6 right at first announcement, 21 eventually found the rule. Mean ratio of incompatible to compatible tests was 1.79 for first-time-right versus 0.24 for first-time-wrong; among those who failed first, 0.50 for second-time-right and 0.19 for those still wrong.
limits: Described second-hand in the LLM paper; the 1960 article itself was not opened. Later work (Klayman and Ha 1987) argues positive testing is not the same as confirmation bias.
agent_relevance: This is the root paradigm for S7: test where two rules differ, not where they agree.

source: Klayman and Ha (1987) Confirmation, disconfirmation and information in hypothesis testing, as described in Jhaveri et al. (2026) and Batista and Griffiths (2026)
finding: A positive test strategy (test cases your hypothesis says are true) is often a good heuristic and approximates optimal information gathering when the target is narrower than the hypothesis. It fails when the hidden rule is broader, as in 2-4-6.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Second-hand only. The original paper was not opened.
agent_relevance: The right test is the one that discriminates between rival rules, not a rule of always disconfirm. Match test type to the relative size of the hypotheses.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky and Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: evaluating and mitigating confirmation bias in language models
finding: Eleven LLMs played the 2-4-6 rule-discovery game (propose a triple, get feedback, guess the rule, up to 45 turns). Models propose confirming triples and discover rules slowly. Confirmation bias is measured as the ratio of incompatible to compatible tests (I:C).
numbers: Task success ranged from 6% to 78%. Qwen3-8B success about 6% in standard mode; 80 episodes per model-variant. Significant positive correlation between I:C and success for thinking and non-thinking models.
limits: Uses Wason's original broad-rule setup, where positive testing is a poor strategy; the authors note the later critique.
agent_relevance: Directly supports the claim that LLMs also prefer confirming tests. S7 should force at least one test the current best answer predicts will fail.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky and Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: evaluating and mitigating confirmation bias in language models
finding: Two prompts from human work cut confirmation bias: Think-in-Opposites (consider counterexamples) and Dual-Goal (rule A versus rule B). On average, rule discovery rose from 42% to 56%. Think-in-Opposites improved success in all scenarios; Dual-Goal in 8 of 11.
numbers: I:C rose in 18 of 22 cases. Paired permutation tests with 50,000 permutations, Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Significant for thinking models; mixed for non-thinking models (no significant I:C change).
limits: Effects are significant for reasoning models only. Switching to thinking mode raised success without raising I:C, so thinking is not the same as testing negatively.
agent_relevance: Use counterexample prompting at S7 only with a reasoning-capable model, and verify by counting incompatible tests in code.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky and Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: evaluating and mitigating confirmation bias in language models
finding: Distilling the counterexample behaviour into the model transferred to a different task (Blicket-style object testing) and to better self-correction in math.
numbers: Students Qwen3-8B and 32B trained on Wason traces generated under intervention; improvements shown in the Blicket domain and in math revision.
limits: Distillation changes weights, which our scaffold cannot do.
agent_relevance: Confirms the behaviour is learnable, but for a scaffold-only agent the lever is the prompt plus code-checked test selection.

source: Batista and Griffiths (2026) A rational analysis of the effects of sycophantic AI
finding: Modified 2-4-6 task with 557 Prolific participants, each talking to a GPT-5.1-Chat agent that supplied example sequences. Bayesian analysis says confirming data raise confidence without moving toward the truth. The default chatbot behaved like a confirming source.
numbers: Discovery rate: random sequences from the true rule 29.5%; Rule Disconfirming 14.1%; Agreeable 11.8%; Rule Confirming 8.4%; Default GPT 5.9%. Default versus random: difference 23.6 percentage points, 95% CI [-34.0, -13.2].
limits: Human participants, one model, one rule, online sample; final hypotheses scored by an LLM coder. Disconfirming versus confirming was not significant (p=.143).
agent_relevance: A model that picks test cases from its own current belief is a confirming source. At S7, let code or an independent sampler draw the test inputs.

source: Batista and Griffiths (2026) A rational analysis of the effects of sycophantic AI
finding: The paper gives a rational account of why testing only inside your hypothesis fails: the evidence is sampled from the hypothesis, so the posterior barely moves while certainty grows.
numbers: Pre-registered, five between-participant conditions, N=504 with a final hypothesis; chi-square(4)=28.02, p<.001 for differences across conditions.
limits: The Bayesian account is a model, not an LLM measurement.
agent_relevance: Gives the formal reason the generator should not also pick the discriminating test.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori and Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: evaluating inductive reasoning in LLMs with rule discovery games
finding: Twelve LLMs discover hidden semantic properties through test examples (100 games each). Reasoning models beat instruction-tuned models, but none is near optimal. Negative testing is the main driver of success.
numbers: Success: GPT-5.2-Chat 75%, GPT-OSS-120B 68%, best instruction-tuned (DeepSeek-V3.1) 41%, other instruction-tuned 33% to 35%; small models GPT-5-Nano 12% and Qwen3.5-9B 21%.
limits: Task is semantic categories (WordNet) with an LLM as oracle; oracle accuracy 85% to 95% against human labels.
agent_relevance: Quantifies the gap: even strong models fail to falsify, so S7 is worth building.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori and Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: evaluating inductive reasoning in LLMs with rule discovery games
finding: Across 12 models, the share of positive tests correlates strongly negatively with conclusive falsifications.
numbers: Spearman rho = -0.937, p < 0.001. Conclusive falsification rate: GPT-OSS-20B 59.2%, GPT-OSS-120B 53.4%, GPT-5.2-Chat 49.5%, Llama-4-Maverick 18.0%, GPT-5-Nano 26.6%.
limits: The paper notes negative testing is not always the better strategy; it fits here because the true rule is often more general than the guess.
agent_relevance: Track the rate of conclusive falsifications as the S7 health metric.

source: Banatt, Cheng, Vaidyanath and Hwu (2024) WILT: a multi-turn, memorization-robust inductive logic benchmark for LLMs
finding: Benchmark based on 2-4-6: a hidden Boolean function over three numbers, up to 30 test cases, binary feedback, then a guess. Best model scored low.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 14/50 (28%); o1-mini 13/50; o1-preview 12/50; GPT-4o 9/50; Llama 3.1 405B 8/50; GPT-4o-mini 6/50; Gemini 1.5 Pro 5/50.
limits: 50 tasks; 2024-era models; tasks are numeric.
agent_relevance: Shows that, before reasoning-model gains, LLMs had low accuracy at choosing informative tests.

source: Wang, Ihlamur and Alican (2025) SSFF: LLM predictive capabilities for startup success through a multi-agent framework
finding: Baseline LLMs given only founder information and a short description (under 100 words) over-predict startup success. GPT-4o had perfect recall but precision 21.28% and accuracy 26.00%. This is an untested-assumption failure: the model trusts founder claims.
numbers: 50 startups (40 unsuccessful, 10 successful). Accuracy: GPT-4o 26%, GPT-4o-mini 24%, SSFF-4o 34%, SSFF-4o-mini 50% (recall 90%, precision 27.27%).
limits: Tiny stratified sample; authors are from a VC firm that sells the tool; 50% is below the 80% a model gets by always saying unsuccessful.
agent_relevance: LLMs accept plans at face value. An assumption-listing step that asks what must be true before approval attacks that bias, but SSFF does not do this test itself.

source: Otis, Clarke, Delecourt, Holtz and Koning (2024) The uneven impact of generative AI on entrepreneurial performance
finding: Field RCT with 640 Kenyan entrepreneurs: GPT-4 mentor over WhatsApp versus a standard business guide. Overall effect on revenue and profit: null, with large spread by baseline performance.
numbers: Low performers -0.09 s.d. (p=0.007, 95% CI [-0.15,-0.03]), about a 10% drop; high performers +0.19 s.d. (p=0.07), about a 15% gain; difference 0.267 s.d. (p=0.013). 634 of 640 completed.
limits: High-performer effect is weak (p=0.07). Not an assumption-testing intervention; shows what generic AI advice does.
agent_relevance: Plain AI advice with no test step does not reliably help; low performers asked harder questions and got advice that sounded good but did not solve the problem.

source: Otis, Clarke, Delecourt, Holtz and Koning (2024) The uneven impact of generative AI on entrepreneurial performance
finding: Log analysis: both groups used the mentor about equally (high performers sent 0.59 more messages, p=0.33). Low performers asked about harder tasks.
numbers: Average difference in messages 0.59, p=0.33.
limits: Exploratory analysis only.
agent_relevance: Route harder, higher-uncertainty questions through an explicit test step rather than free advice.

source: Search summary of practitioner sources on riskiest-assumption testing (Bland and Osterwalder, Testing Business Ideas)
finding: Search found no academic paper where an LLM lists assumptions, ranks them by risk and cost, and tests them, with measured outcomes. Bland and Osterwalder rank assumptions by importance and by how little evidence supports them.
numbers: No measured results found. R.A.I.S.E. (arXiv 2504.12090) and SSFF address startup evaluation, not assumption testing.
limits: Evidence gap, from one search. Not opened.
agent_relevance: A gap: our S7 design for ranking and testing assumptions would be new, so it should be measured against a plain baseline.
